source.title: What Drives Representation Steering? A Mechanistic Case Study on Steering Refusal
source.authors: Stephen Cheng; Sarah Wiegreffe; Dinesh Manocha

page_placements.theme: Where the direction acts: template positions, layers, pathways and upstream features

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present, although some tables and equations are flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The study computes difference-in-means refusal vectors and applies positive and negative activation steering, then evaluates refusal-related ASR on three models. This directly reproduces the steering part of V1 on additional models, but it does not perform the claimed projection ablation of the direction.
record.gate_note: Table 2 reports DIM steering and unsteered ASR on harmless Alpaca and harmful JailbreakBench and StrongReject prompts; these rows bear on V1’s addition/steering behavior. Table 1 reports ASR after ablations of components involved in propagating DIM steering, not projection of the refusal direction itself; those component results are recorded under fits_no_version. The study also reports NTP/PO steering results and sparsification analyses, but they do not test the listed versions’ claims about the DIM direction. Perplexity is reported for DIM sparsification, not as a task-based general-capability evaluation.
record.test_reason: Computes the Arditi-style difference-in-means refusal vector, selected by the original's procedure, on three new instruct models. It reports refusal and jailbreak rates on Alpaca, JailbreakBench and StrongReject, judged by substring matching and LlamaGuard 2, with and without adding (α=1) or subtracting (α=−1) the vector (Appendix B.1, Table 2). This replicates V1's induce/bypass steering result. It does not report directional ablation outcomes: ablation enters only as a KL constraint during vector selection. The rest of the paper is circuit analysis of the steering pathway.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that refusal steering vectors from different methods use highly overlapping, interchangeable circuits at the same layer. Steering acts on attention mainly via OV rather than QK: freezing attention scores costs only 8.83%. The steering value vector decomposition is interpretable, and vectors can be sparsified 85–96% with most performance retained.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the difference-in-means vector and activation addition/subtraction as in the original, but studies multi-token steering at selected layers and extends the evaluation to three models and circuit interventions; it does not perform the original direction-projection ablation.
record.method_sensitivity: The analysis uses the selected best DIM layer for each model (Gemma 2 2B layer 15, Llama 3.2 3B layer 12, Qwen 3 8B layer 20); steering polarity and evaluation set differ between harmless and harmful prompts. The authors state they do not evaluate vectors at other layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Freezing QK attention during DIM steering barely changes the steering effect (avg 8.83%). Freezing OV, removing the direct value-vector term (SVV), or removing the direct MLP input cuts the effect by 45–64% on average.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The refusal direction's steering effect propagates mainly through attention OV/value pathways and MLPs, not through attention patterns.

fits_no_version.finding: Learned NTP and PO refusal vectors have only 0.10–0.42 cosine similarity to DIM, yet steer refusal about as well (Table 2). They also use ≳90% overlapping, interchangeable circuits (§5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Several fairly dissimilar directions at one layer steer refusal equally through a shared circuit. This bears loosely on V4 but is not a test of cone or multi-direction structure.

fits_no_version.finding: DIM vectors sparsified to 85–96% zeroed dimensions keep most steering ASR. On Llama, 9 of 3072 dimensions keep StrongReject ASR within about 5 points (Tables 8–10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal steering is driven by a small subset of residual dimensions shared across vector-learning methods.

record.peer_reviewed: Accepted as a main conference paper at EMNLP 2026
record.problems: The study does not project the DIM refusal direction out of the residual stream, so its central component ablations do not directly test the claimed directional ablation. The study evaluates vectors only at the selected DIM layer and does not test other layers. No uncertainty estimates are given for the ASR results. Perplexity is reported for sparsification, but there is no task-based general-capability evaluation.
record.rows_left_out: NTP and PO results in Appendix B.1, Table 2, and detailed DIM/NTP/PO sparsification results in Figures 6 and 10 and Tables 8–10 were not extracted as rows because they concern alternative learned vectors or sparsification rather than the listed DIM-direction versions. Perplexity results in Table 7 are not task-based capability measures and concern sparsified vectors rather than the dense-direction steering test.

untested.parts: Projection ablation of the direction at every layer and position, and its effect on refusal. Task-based preservation of other abilities. Only addition and subtraction at a single selected layer were tested.
No analysis of jailbreak prompts or adversarial training.
No test of affine, cone or multi-direction structure.
Not tested. Logit-lens tokens mix harm and refusal concepts, but there is no separation test.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer.
Qwen 3 8B was evaluated only in non-thinking mode.

missing.what: Pile and Alpaca perplexity with the dense DIM vector versus no steering: Gemma Pile 12.84→17.63, Llama 11.99→15.79, Qwen 9.45→11.45. This is a cost of steering relevant to V1's 'other abilities kept' clause, though it is not a task-based check and the steering sign is unclear.
NTP and PO learned-vector steering ASR on Gemma and Llama, compared with DIM.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is mainly a mechanistic study of how DIM steering propagates. Only Table 2 bears directly on the claim, and only on V1's addition/subtraction half. Directional ablation appears solely as a KL selection constraint, with no reported ablation ASR. The component ablations (Table 1) ablate pathways of the steering signal, not the direction, so they are correctly not linked to V1. Rows r25–r33 are redundant baselines. Peer-review status was taken from the header as stated; dates in the text look future-dated.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests adding and subtracting a DIM steering vector, but not projecting that direction out of every layer and position. It does not establish that other abilities remain largely intact.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
No test of whether jailbreak attacks suppress the direction, or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
No test of affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal.
No test separating harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Vectors are obtained and tested within each model; cross-language or cross-model transfer is not tested.
The study compares steering-vector learning methods, not how refusal-alignment training determines whether a removable direction exists.
Qwen 3 8B is tested in non-thinking mode; no reasoning-before-answering model setting is tested.

relationships.reason: Harmless compliance falls from ≥0.99 to ≤0.03 (r34, r37, r40). Harmful ASR rises from ≤0.04 to 0.80–0.89 (r35, r36, r38, r39, r41, r42). This covers steering only, not ablation.
relationships.display_finding: Addition reduced harmless compliance from ≥0.99 to ≤0.03, while subtraction increased harmful attack success from ≤0.04 to 0.80–0.89.

relation.reason: Table 2 reports refusal and ASR rates, unsteered against DIM-steered, on held-out Alpaca, JailbreakBench and StrongReject for three models. That is the study's own result on whether the direction mediates refusal, even though the paper's focus is mechanistic.

tranche.reason: Same DIM vector, chosen by Arditi's selection procedure (slightly changed, Appendix B.1). Same addition to induce refusal, same substring judge and LlamaGuard 2, on new models. Bypass uses subtraction rather than directional ablation, which the record's verdict fixes already flag.

source_check.notes: Table 7 (Appendix G.4) gives Pile/Alpaca perplexity under dense DIM steering. Pile rises 12.84→17.63 (G2), 11.99→15.79 (L3), 9.45→11.45 (Q8); the steering sign is not stated. This bears on V1's 'other abilities kept', and none of the checked rows hold it. Alpaca test n is 100, augmented to 200 for sparse evaluations. Q8's 0.995/0.015 imply n=200. No uncertainty is given for ASR.
